passages.t: The alarm, and an army like no other
passages.happening:
Blow the ram's horn in Zion and sound the alarm on God's holy mountain. Let everyone in the land tremble, ‘for the Day of the LORD is coming; indeed, it is near’ (verse 1). It is a day of darkness and gloom. Like dawn spreading over the mountains, a great and strong army appears, such as never was before (verse 2).

Fire goes before it. The land in front is like the Garden of Eden, and behind it a desert (verse 3). They look like horses and run like warhorses, with a sound like chariots (verses 4-5). They charge like warriors, scale the walls, keep their ranks, and climb into houses through the windows like thieves (verses 7-9). The earth quakes, and the sun, moon and stars grow dark (verse 10). ‘The LORD raises His voice in the presence of His army’ (verse 11). The Day of the LORD is great and very dreadful. ‘Who can endure it?’
passages.hearers:
Chapter 1 described a locust plague and named it a sign of the Day of the LORD. Chapter 2 brings that Day into full view. The ram's horn was blown to sound alarms in war and to call the people to holy gatherings. Here, in verse 1, it sounds the alarm.

Interpreters differ over the army. Many read it as the locusts of chapter 1 pictured as an army, since the details fit locust swarms closely: the look of horses, climbing walls, coming in at windows. Others see a human invader, perhaps Assyrian or Babylonian, described with locust pictures, pointing to the northern army of verse 20, since Israel's great invaders came from the north. Still others read it as a force at the end of days, the last showing of the Day of the LORD. The pictures blur these on purpose, and each reading has able defenders.

The most frightening line is the last. The army is the LORD's own. He leads it. That is why the question, who can endure it, has no answer except the one that comes next.
passages.later: Amos asked the same question of those who longed for that day: ‘It will be darkness and not light’ (Amos 5:18). The army is pictured with the darkened sun, moon and stars that other prophets use for God's great acts (Isaiah 13:10).
passages.asks: Joel says the army belongs to the LORD. Ask how you feel about a God who cannot be managed or tamed. And ask what in your own life would not survive his coming close.

passages.t: Yet even now: return with all your heart
passages.happening:
The turn begins with the words ‘Yet even now’ (verse 12). The LORD calls his people to return to him with all their heart, with fasting, weeping and mourning. ‘So rend your hearts and not your garments, and return to the LORD your God. For He is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion. And He relents from sending disaster’ (verse 13). ‘Who knows? He may turn and relent’ (verse 14), and leave grain and drink offerings for the LORD.

Blow the ram's horn again and call a sacred assembly (verse 15). Gather everyone: the old, the children, babies at the breast. Let the bridegroom leave his room and the bride her chamber (verse 16). Let the priests weep between the porch and the altar and pray that the LORD will spare his people and not let them become a mockery among the nations (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
This is the turning point of the whole book. The same prophet who sounded the alarm now says it is not too late. Tearing one's clothes was a traditional sign of grief or shock. Joel does not abolish the sign. He demands that it express a real change inside. Rend your hearts.

Verse 13 quotes the ancient confession of God's character, first spoken to Moses at Sinai and repeated in the psalms and in Jonah. The people return not to an unknown power but to a God who has said who he is.

The call to gather even nursing babies and couples on their wedding day shows a crisis grave enough to override every other duty. The law normally excused a new husband from military service for a year. The priests were to weep between the porch at the front of the temple and the altar, the place where they usually served. This time the horn of verse 15 calls the people to worship, not to war.
passages.later: God proclaimed his name to Moses: ‘The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness’ (Exodus 34:6). Jonah quoted the same words, angry that God had relented (Jonah 4:2). The law excused a new husband from war for a year (Deuteronomy 24:5).
passages.asks: God asks for torn hearts, not torn clothes. Ask whether your sorrow for sin has stayed on the outside. And ask what it means that the call is ‘Yet even now’, even after so much has been lost.

passages.t: The LORD answers, and repays the lost years
passages.happening:
‘Then the LORD became jealous for His land, and He spared His people’ (verse 18). He answers that he will send grain, new wine and oil, and never again make them a mockery among the nations (verse 19). He will drive the northern army away, into a barren land and into the seas, and its stench will rise (verse 20).

The land is not to fear, nor the animals, for the pastures are green and the fig and vine bear fruit (verses 21-22). The children of Zion are to rejoice, for God has given the autumn rains and sends the spring rains as before (verse 23). The threshing floors will be full and the vats will overflow (verse 24). ‘I will repay you for the years eaten by locusts’ (verse 25). They will eat and be satisfied, and know that the LORD is among them, ‘and there is no other’ (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
Verse 18 is the hinge of the book. Everything after it is God's answer, and it reverses chapter 1 point by point. Grain, new wine and oil return. The fig and vine bear fruit. The animals that panted for water find green pasture. The four locust names are listed again as God promises to repay what they destroyed.

The rains were the lifeblood of Judah's farming year. The autumn rains, roughly October and November, softened the ground for plowing and sowing, and the spring rains, roughly March and April, filled out the grain before harvest. The word rendered autumn rains in verse 23 can also mean teacher, and some interpreters read the teacher for righteousness; most translations prefer rain.

The Eastern Sea and the Western Sea are the Dead Sea and the Mediterranean. Locust swarms that died in the sea could wash ashore and rot, which may explain the stench of verse 20.
passages.later: The law had promised rain in its season for a faithful people: ‘then I will provide rain for your land in season, the autumn and spring rains’ (Deuteronomy 11:14). Hosea promised the same answering of heaven and earth (Hosea 2:21-22).
passages.asks: God promises to repay the years the locusts ate. Ask what years in your life feel eaten, and what it would mean to bring them to God. And ask whether you are waiting for restoration, or for the God who restores.

passages.happening:
‘And afterward, I will pour out My Spirit on all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy, your old men will dream dreams, your young men will see visions’ (verse 28). ‘Even on My menservants and maidservants, I will pour out My Spirit in those days’ (verse 29).

God will show wonders in the heavens and on the earth, blood and fire and columns of smoke (verse 30). The sun will turn dark and the moon to blood before the great and awesome Day of the LORD (verse 31). ‘And everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved’ (verse 32), for on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be deliverance, among the remnant the LORD calls.
passages.hearers:
In Israel's history the Spirit had come on particular people, prophets, judges and kings, for particular tasks. Moses once wished that all the LORD's people were prophets. Joel promises it. The Spirit will come on all kinds of people, without regard to age, sex or rank: sons and daughters, old and young, even servants, men and women.

Afterward places this after the restoration of the land. The wonders that follow are the usual language of the prophets for God breaking into history, and they lead to the great Day. In the middle of all that, the promise is simple: everyone who calls on the LORD's name will be saved.

In the Hebrew Bible these five verses form a chapter of their own, chapter 3.
passages.later: Moses said, ‘I wish that all the LORD’s people were prophets’ (Numbers 11:29). At Pentecost Peter told the crowd, ‘No, this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel’ (Acts 2:16), and quoted these verses. Paul quotes verse 32 for Jew and Gentile alike: ‘Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved’ (Romans 10:13).
passages.hard:
Peter said this was fulfilled at Pentecost, but the sun did not turn dark or the moon to blood that day. How does that work?

Interpreters answer in several ways. Some note that the sun was darkened at Jesus' crucifixion only weeks earlier (Luke 23:44-45), and suggest that Peter saw the signs as already under way. Others read the signs as the prophets' usual language for God's decisive acts in history, pictures of upheaval rather than forecasts of the sky, as when Isaiah uses similar words for the fall of Babylon (Isaiah 13:10). Many see the fulfillment as beginning at Pentecost and completed at Christ's return: the Spirit's coming marks the start of the last days, and the signs belong to the great Day still to come.

These views can overlap. They share the conviction that Peter was right to see Joel's promised age of the Spirit arriving in the church. What Peter stressed was the Spirit's coming and the offer of salvation, not a timetable of signs in the sky.
passages.asks: The Spirit is promised to sons and daughters, old and young, servants and free. Ask who you have assumed God would not speak through. And ask what it would mean for you to call on the name of the Lord today.
